reading.body:
CoreSpace Dallas is a 30,000 square foot data center facility in Dallas, Texas with no publicly disclosed power capacity.

The absence of a power specification for this facility is notable. Most data centers list their capacity in megawatts as a basic operational parameter, either because it defines their market positioning or because colocation and cloud customers need to know it before committing workloads. CoreSpace's choice not to publish this figure on their site leaves the facility's role in the regional compute ecosystem unclear. It could serve a specific customer or use case that does not require public transparency, or the capacity may be modest relative to hyperscaler facilities in the same region.

This gap illustrates a broader challenge in mapping AI infrastructure: not all facilities that support compute workloads disclose their power draw or capacity. A 30,000 square foot building in a major metropolitan area like Dallas represents real physical infrastructure that consumes electricity and enables computation, but without the power metric, its contribution to regional grid load remains unquantified. For tracking whether the grid constrains AI scaling in Texas, these undisclosed facilities matter because they are load that demand-side forecasting must account for even when supply-side data is incomplete.
